title: Welcoming guests
hookLine: hospitality from Abraham's tent onward (Genesis 18): water, bread, and running to meet the stranger
tomorrow: a law said pray to no one but the king. why did he open his window?

lines: THE HEAT OF THE DAY, A TENT DOOR.
cards: The heat of the day, a tent door, an old man sitting in it.

Genesis 18: "he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day; And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door". Abraham, in the heat, runs.

He bows, and offers a little water to wash their feet, a rest under the tree, a morsel of bread. Then he hurries to Sarah: "Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth."
He runs to the herd for a calf, brings butter and milk, and stands by them under the tree while they eat.

teach.b: Smell the bread on the hearth; feel cool water on dusty feet. The story is all senses, and the guests turn out to be messengers of God.
Jewish teaching made a commandment of what Abraham did: hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests. The Talmud draws a bold line from this chapter.
It opens with the LORD appearing to Abraham, and then Abraham turns and runs to the strangers, so the rabbis say that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.
The Letter to the Hebrews, in the New Testament, looks back at the same tent: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

teach.h: WATER, BREAD, AND STAYING BY THEM.
teach.b: And the Qur'an tells of Abraham's guests and the calf he brought them too. In each of these tellings, the stranger at the door might be heaven's messenger.
A welcome isn't the décor. It's the water, the bread, and staying by them while they eat.

how: Jews treat welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, as a commandment learned from Abraham; Christians cite Hebrews 13:2, and Muslims also tell of Abraham's guests.

o: opening your door and table to someone, even a stranger
keeping your home private so guests feel no pressure
inviting only close family to the big holiday meals

games.q: the tent at Mamre: tap the pairs.
p: where Abraham sat in the heat of the day

s: Abraham waited for the strangers to ask for help
he saw them and ran to meet them from the tent door.
the Talmud says welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence
the rabbis read it from Abraham turning from God to greet the three.

games.q: Theo shows up early to your dinner, sweaty from biking over, while you're still cooking. what does Abraham's tent suggest first?
o: hand him water and a seat; the welcome starts before the meal is ready.
send him for a walk until the table is set, so it's done properly.
keep cooking; the guest is honored by the meal, not the greeting.
games.why: Abraham's first offer was a little water, rest under the tree, and a morsel of bread; the feast came after.

practice: Get up and walk, at an easy pace, to the door of the room you're in. Stand in the doorway for a breath or two, the way Abraham sat in his tent door, looking out.
Then come back, sit, and let one person come to mind whom you could invite in, to your table or just your doorstep.

wordCard.voice: Welcoming guests: water, bread, and running to the door. Jews call it hachnasat orchim, and it begins at Abraham's tent.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing in guests, the Jewish commandment drawn from Abraham's tent.

carryVoice: The line to keep: Abraham's tent, where an old man ran out in the heat to meet strangers. The door's open.
